title: Report on Studying at the Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: I have recently studied abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk (hereafter MUG) in Gdansk, Poland, and I would like to report on it. Gdansk is the largest port city in Poland, on the Baltic Sea, a beautiful city with a medieval air, and at the same time a historically important city as the place where the Second World War broke out and as a center of the democratisation of the Eastern European countries. Perhaps it will feel a little more familiar if I say that the soccer player 松井大輔 played there for the local professional team, Lechia Gdansk. I did clerkships for three months, from April to June, in this city so far removed from Nagoya.

The university hospital where I did my clerkships (the Academic Clinical Center) is a core hospital serving a medical area of 3.5 million people, a large hospital with about 1,300 beds and about 21,000 operations a year. A characteristic is that each department has a different building; for example, the building housing surgery and emergency medicine was built only a few years ago and is new, while the obstetrics and gynecology building dates from before the war and is located at a distance. MUG puts effort into international exchange, with the English Division, which educates students from outside Poland in English for six years, and the ERASMUS program for exchange within Europe, and the exchange with Nagoya University, which started from a connection through joint research, also takes place almost every year.

At MUG this time, I wanted to see as many departments as possible, so I did two-week clerkships each in obstetrics and gynecology, family medicine, emergency medicine, cardiology, general surgery and cardiac surgery. In family medicine and emergency medicine, I joined the sixth-year class of the English Division and mainly studied in lecture format. In the other departments, I consulted the doctors in advance by email and so on, and decided the content of the clerkship each time.

In family medicine, I learned about common diseases such as lifestyle-related diseases in PBL format and so on. It was striking that diseases that are not very familiar in Japan, such as celiac disease and Lyme disease, rank high in the differential diagnosis as frequent conditions. Although it was only for one day, I was also allowed to visit a family doctor's clinic and caught a glimpse of the work of a family doctor as a private practitioner.

In emergency medicine I mainly learned ACLS, and there were also unique classes, such as visiting a doctor helicopter and practising triage in class by splitting into disaster victims and a rescue team. The local students were very aggressive: in ACLS, whoever played the doctor could take leadership, and they would interrupt the lecture to argue with the teacher, so I felt the difference from clerkships at Nagoya University.

In cardiology, I was taught individually by the hospital's doctors, and did rounds, observation and case discussions. When there was an English-speaking patient, I was able to take a history and do a physical examination, though only a little.

In obstetrics and gynecology, general surgery and cardiac surgery, I mainly observed surgery and assisted in operations. In every department, what impressed me was that there were few barriers between professions such as doctors and nurses, and little hierarchy among doctors; even nurses voiced their opinions to doctors freely (though it was in Polish so I could hardly understand), and even I as a student was let into surgery as a part of the workforce. The surgeries were mostly endometrial and cervical cancer in obstetrics and gynecology, and CABG (and occasionally left ventricular reconstruction) in cardiac surgery, and it was impressive that CABG was done off-pump. In general surgery, besides various cancers, they performed stomach reduction surgery almost every day for people with morbid obesity (BMI of 40 or more), which is not covered by insurance in Japan, and I felt that I was really doing a clerkship in the West. I mostly took part in surgery as second assistant, but after getting friendly with the doctors to a certain extent, I was sometimes allowed to be first assistant when they were short of hands, and I experienced everything from intubation and urinary catheter insertion to skin suturing, laparotomy and thoracotomy. The surgery was not as careful as in Japan, but very fast, and I was impressed that they worked in a relaxed way while chatting. One doctor taught me, "What you learn here is just 'No music, no surgery,' that's all," and I was able to do my clerkship with great enjoyment.

In daily life, a student dormitory was provided free of charge, supermarkets and department stores were nearby, and prices were the lowest in Europe, so I had no trouble. Also, Professor Wozniak, who was in charge of receiving me, and the other people at the university, as well as the people led by Piotr who had studied at Nagoya University, treated me very well, so I was able to fully enjoy a very comfortable life abroad.

The people who have studied in Gdansk have very strong ties; a send-off party was held for me before departure, and the seniors with experience of studying at MUG gave me all sorts of stories and advice. It was also a great help that a trunk packed with daily necessities was kept in Professor Wozniak's laboratory for students coming from Nagoya University to use freely.

On this study abroad, I experienced many things that I could not have done in Japan, and I was able to spend the most intense time of my university life. I would like to express my sincere thanks to 木下さん, who spent the study abroad in Poland with me, to everyone in the International Exchange Office, who gave me the opportunity to study abroad and supported me before and after it, and to everyone else involved in my study abroad.
